records.title: The Jayuro Ghost with Hollow Sunglasses Eyes
records.summary: Jayuro is a major highway connecting Seoul to Ilsan and Paju along the Han River near the North Korean DMZ, notorious for thick river fog and high-speed commuter traffic. Beginning in the early 2000s, numerous motorists and Korean celebrities reported encountering a slender young woman standing beside the guardrail in dense midnight fog wearing fashionable dark sunglasses. Drivers who slow down to offer assistance recoil in horror when headlights illuminate her face: she is not wearing sunglasses, but has hollow, gouged-out black sockets in place of her eyes, staring blankly into passing vehicles.
records.historical_period: Early 2000s to Present (major broadcast television investigations 2007)

records.title: The Haunted Gonjiam Psychiatric Hospital
records.summary: Located in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, the Gonjiam Psychiatric Hospital opened in 1992 and was abruptly abandoned in 1996 due to water supply issues and financial disputes. However, viral Korean netlore transformed the abandoned concrete ruins into a house of horrors, alleging that the asylum director went insane and performed illegal experiments, leading to mass suicides of patients. Listed by CNN Travel in 2012 as one of the '7 Freakiest Places on the Planet' and immortalized in the 2018 horror film 'Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum,' thousands of nocturnal urban explorers reported slamming iron doors, disembodied screams, and icy chills until the building was demolished in 2018.
alternate_names: The Haunted Psychiatric Hospital of Gwangju

records.title: Red Paper or Blue Paper Bathroom Spirit (Ppalgan Hyuji Paran Hyuji)
records.summary: A ubiquitous fixture of South Korean primary and middle school ghostlore since the 1980s, this legend centers on older school restrooms. A student sitting in the final toilet stall discovers there is no toilet paper, when a sinister, disembodied hand reaches up through the toilet pit holding two rolls of paper, asking: 'Do you want red paper or blue paper?' (Ppalgan hyuji julkka, paran hyuji julkka?). Choosing red causes the spirit to slit the victim's throat so blood covers their body; choosing blue causes the spirit to strangle the victim until their face turns cyan blue. The only survival trick taught by schoolyard lore is to shout: 'I don't need any paper!' and sprint out.
alternate_names: The Red and Blue Toilet Paper Ghost

records.title: The Fan Death Phenomenon (Seonpunggi Samang)
records.summary: Unique to South Korea and treated as a serious public health matter throughout the late 20th century, 'Fan Death' (Seonpunggi Samang) is the widespread belief that sleeping in a sealed room with an electric fan running will lead to asphyxiation, hypothermia, or carbon dioxide poisoning. Heavily reinforced by mainstream South Korean news media reports, government safety warnings, and medical advisories from the 1970s through the 1990s, Korean electric fan manufacturers universally install mechanical shutdown timers and auto-shutoff features to reassure worried consumers.
records.region_or_community: Nationwide South Korean society and medical folklore
geographic_associations: Urban residential apartments throughout South Korea

records.title: The Bongcheon-dong Ghost Webcomic Spectre
records.summary: In July 2011, Korean webtoon artist Studio Horang published a viral Naver webcomic based on a popular local Seoul urban legend from the Bongcheon-dong apartment complex in Gwanak-gu. The story describes a high school student walking home late through the high-rise apartment corridors who encounters an unnaturally contorted woman in pink pajamas with twisted limbs and disheveled hair, limping forward and asking: 'Where is my baby?' Utilizing automated script triggers that made the horrifying face pop out with cracking joint sound effects, the digital legend terrified millions worldwide, becoming a defining icon of modern Korean digital horror.

records.title: The Ghost Station of Sinseol-dong Underground
records.summary: Constructed in the 1970s as part of Seoul Subway Line 1 and 2 expansion plans, the sealed, abandoned underground platform beneath Sinseol-dong Station is known as Seoul's definitive 'Ghost Station' (Yuryeong Yeok). Disconnected from regular commercial passenger traffic and shrouded in complete darkness, maintenance workers and film crews authorized to shoot music videos report sudden temperature drops, flickering electrical lights, and shadowy figures of commuters waiting on the dusty tracks where no train ever stops.

records.title: The Bleeding Tears of King Sejong's Statue
records.summary: Dominating Gwanghwamun Plaza in central Seoul before Gyeongbokgung Palace, the colossal bronze statue of King Sejong the Great, who created the Korean Hangul alphabet in 1443, is the focus of patriotic and supernatural urban legends. According to Seoul civic folklore, during periods of acute national crisis, political turmoil, or impending tragedy on the Korean Peninsula, security cameras and nocturnal tourists have reported seeing dark streaks resembling weeping blood trickling down the bronze cheeks of the wise king, interpreted as the ancestral sovereign weeping for his descendants.

records.title: The Elevator Game to Another Dimension
records.summary: Originating in South Korean internet occult chatrooms and popularized on Japanese forums in the late 2000s, 'The Elevator Game' is a complex supernatural ritual claimed to transport a solitary player to an alternate dimension. The player must enter an empty elevator in a building at least ten stories high and press buttons in a precise sequence: 4-2-6-2-10-5. On the 5th floor, a mysterious young woman enters the car; the player is strictly warned never to look at her or speak to her. If the player then presses 1 and the elevator instead ascends to the 10th floor, they have successfully arrived in the 'Other World'—a desolate, red-hued mirror version of reality with no electricity and glowing crimson windows.

records.title: The Drowned Maiden of Cheonggyecheon Stream
records.summary: Flowing through the heart of downtown Seoul, Cheonggyecheon was a historic Joseon waterway covered by elevated concrete expressways during the post-war industrial boom, before being spectacularly restored in 2005 as an urban public park. In Seoul ghostlore, before the restoration when the stream was a dark subterranean concrete culvert, numerous impoverished shantytown residents and workers drowned during sudden monsoon flash floods. Night stroll couples walking along the illuminated stone walkways near Gwangtonggyo Bridge report hearing feminine weeping from the dark water culverts and seeing wet footprints appearing on the stone steps that dissolve into mist.
records.historical_period: Post-War industrial era to Post-2005 stream restoration

records.title: The Cursed Mirror of Yeongdeungpo Market
records.summary: In the historic labyrinthine corridors of Yeongdeungpo Traditional Market in southwestern Seoul, an antique full-length vanity mirror in an underground secondhand shop is the subject of eerie merchant lore. Legend claims the mirror belonged to a wealthy Joseon courtesan who perished during the Korean War. Shopkeepers allege that visitors who stand alone before the mirror at 3:00 AM while lighting a match will see their own reflection delay its movements by three seconds, before smiling back with sunken, empty black eyes, triggering intense psychological dread and temporary paralysis.
